name: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)

matching.reasoningTemplate: Isolated thrombocytopenia with mucocutaneous bleeding in a well patient suggests ITP.

redFlags: Major bleeding / very low platelets need urgent treatment

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.921-924 (Chap. 120, Disorders of Platelets and Vessel Wall)
clinicalPearls: ITP is an acquired disorder of immune-mediated platelet destruction, with possible additional inhibition of platelet release from megakaryocytes (p.924).
In children ITP is usually acute, often follows an infection, and is self-limited; in adults it tends to be chronic, though some adults remit spontaneously within months of diagnosis (p.924).
It is largely a diagnosis of exclusion: characterized by mucocutaneous bleeding and a low (often very low) platelet count with otherwise normal peripheral blood cells and smear (p.924).
Presentation is either with ecchymoses/petechiae or with thrombocytopenia found incidentally on a routine CBC (p.924).
Mucocutaneous bleeding may include oral mucosal, gastrointestinal, or heavy menstrual bleeding; rarely life-threatening (including CNS) bleeding occurs (p.924).
Wet purpura (blood blisters in the mouth) and retinal hemorrhages may herald life-threatening bleeding (p.924, p.922).

Petechiae are pinpoint, nonblanching hemorrhages that signal decreased platelet number rather than platelet dysfunction, and first appear in dependent areas of increased venous pressure (ankles/feet in an ambulatory patient) (p.922).
Serologic (antiplatelet antibody) testing is generally not helpful because of low sensitivity and specificity of current tests (p.924).
The peripheral smear may show large platelets with otherwise normal morphology, reflecting young/rapidly turned-over platelets (p.924, p.916).
harrison.pathophysiology: ITP results from immune-mediated destruction of antibody-coated platelets by the reticuloendothelial system, and possibly impaired platelet release from megakaryocytes. Primary ITP has no identifiable cause; secondary ITP is associated with an underlying disorder such as autoimmune disease (notably SLE) or infection (HIV, hepatitis C). Childhood ITP commonly follows a viral infection through immune mechanisms and usually resolves spontaneously (Harrison 22e p.922, p.924).
additionalDifferentials: Drug-induced thrombocytopenia (e.g., quinine, sulfonamides, vancomycin; classic drug-dependent antibodies react with platelet antigens only when drug is present) (p.922-923)
Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) - associated with thrombosis rather than bleeding, nadir rarely <20,000/uL; use 4T scoring (p.923)
Congenital/inherited thrombocytopenia (e.g., autosomal dominant macrothrombocytopenia) (p.922, p.965 algorithm)
Pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping (EDTA-dependent) - redraw in sodium citrate or heparin (p.922, p.965 algorithm)
Evans syndrome - combined autoimmune hemolytic anemia with ITP (perform direct antiglobulin/Coombs test if anemia present) (p.924)
infectionMimics: HIV infection - can cause immune thrombocytopenia early; late HIV causes pancytopenia with decreased/dysplastic platelet production (p.922)
Hepatitis C virus infection - recognized cause of secondary ITP (p.924)
Systemic infection with gram-negative bacteria or COVID-19 - thrombocytopenia that may be associated with DIC (p.922)
Helicobacter pylori - association with ITP is unclear but appears to have a geographic distribution (p.924)
nonInfectiousMimics: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (TTP, DIC) - distinguished by schistocytes/fragmented red cells on smear (p.922, p.965 algorithm)
Hypersplenism/splenomegaly (e.g., chronic liver disease) causing platelet sequestration (p.922)
Bone marrow production failure - low platelet count with absence of large young platelets on smear (p.916, p.922)
additionalInvestigations: CBC with peripheral blood smear review to confirm isolated thrombocytopenia and exclude clumping/schistocytes (p.922, p.924)
HIV and hepatitis C testing to evaluate for secondary ITP (p.924)
Serum protein electrophoresis and immunoglobulin levels (to detect hypogammaglobulinemia or monoclonal gammopathy) (p.924)
H. pylori testing depending on clinical circumstance (p.924)
Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test if anemia present, to detect Evans syndrome (p.924)
Bone marrow examination reserved for patients with unexplained additional findings or failure to respond to initial therapy (p.924)
redFlags: Wet purpura (oral blood blisters) - may herald life-threatening bleeding (p.924, p.922)
Retinal hemorrhages - may herald life-threatening bleeding (p.924)
Active mucosal, GI, or CNS bleeding (p.924)
Very severe thrombocytopenia (<5000/uL) or signs of impending bleeding (p.924)
harrison.prognosis: Childhood ITP is usually acute and almost always resolves spontaneously. Adult ITP is more often chronic, though some adults remit spontaneously within months. Patients with platelet counts >30,000/uL appear not to have increased mortality related to the thrombocytopenia, so diagnosis does not mandate treatment (Harrison 22e p.924).
pitfalls: Treating presumed ITP without excluding secondary causes (HIV, HCV, SLE, drugs) (p.924).
Relying on antiplatelet antibody serology - low sensitivity/specificity makes it unhelpful for diagnosis (p.924).
Missing pseudothrombocytopenia from EDTA-induced platelet clumping, which produces a falsely low automated count; confirm on smear and redraw in citrate/heparin (p.922, p.916).
Overlooking Evans syndrome - failing to do a Coombs test when anemia accompanies thrombocytopenia (p.924).
Failing to take a careful drug/herbal/OTC history, since drugs are the most common cause of thrombocytopenia (p.922).
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal grading scale. Practical thresholds noted: platelet counts >30,000/uL are not associated with increased mortality; ~5000-10,000/uL is the level needed to maintain microvascular integrity; severe thrombocytopenia is cited as <5000/uL for treatment-decision purposes (Harrison 22e p.922, p.924).
